claim: Thick tracts that exited the ALI-COs stained positive for the pan-axonal marker SMI312 and negative for the dendritic marker MAP2.
source: Thick tracts that exited the ALI-COs stained positive for the pan-axonal marker SMI312 and negative for the dendritic marker MAP2 (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The average extension speed for individual fluorescently labeled axons over several hours was 691 nm/min.
source: We measured the extension speed for individual fluorescently labeled axons over several hours to be an average of 691 nm/min, with a peak pace of nearly 3000 nm/min (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by measurements from live fluorescence microscopy tracking data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The peak pace of axon extension was nearly 3000 nm/min.
source: We measured the extension speed for individual fluorescently labeled axons over several hours to be an average of 691 nm/min, with a peak pace of nearly 3000 nm/min (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by measurements from live fluorescence microscopy tracking data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The average speed of axon extension observed is comparable to previous reports of chicken dorsal-root ganglia.
source: The average speed we observed is comparable to previous reports of chicken dorsal-root ganglia (Ketschek et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison to published literature on chicken dorsal-root ganglia.

claim: Actin filaments in axons are unbranched and longitudinally aligned.
source: We observed unbranched, longitudinally aligned actin filaments, recognizable by their characteristic thickness of 7–9 nm and an apparent pitch of 5–6 nm (Egelman et al., 1982; Figure 2A, orange arrows).
evidence: The claim is supported by cryo-ET observations shown in Figure 2A and comparison to known structural characteristics from literature.

claim: Actin filaments have a characteristic thickness of 7–9 nm and an apparent pitch of 5–6 nm.
source: We observed unbranched, longitudinally aligned actin filaments, recognizable by their characteristic thickness of 7–9 nm and an apparent pitch of 5–6 nm (Egelman et al., 1982; Figure 2A, orange arrows).
evidence: The claim is supported by measurements from cryo-ET data and comparison to published structural data.

claim: Microtubules revealed their individual protofilaments and numerous intraluminal protein densities.
source: Microtubules revealed their individual protofilaments (Figure 2A, magenta arrows), as well as numerous intraluminal protein densities (Garvalov et al., 2006; Foster et al., 2021a).
evidence: The claim is supported by cryo-ET observations shown in Figure 2A and comparison to published literature.

claim: Filaments of about 10 nm in diameter were found in axons.
source: We also found filaments of about 10 nm in diameter (Figure 2A, brown arrows).
evidence: The claim is supported by measurements from cryo-ET data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The 10 nm diameter filaments match the dimensions of neurofilaments such as NF-L, NF-M, and NF-H.
source: These dimensions match those of neurofilaments (NFs) such as NF-L, NF-M, and NF-H (Malka-Gibor et al., 2017), which serve as signature markers for axons.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison to published structural data on neurofilaments.

claim: Neurofilaments serve as signature markers for axons.
source: These dimensions match those of neurofilaments (NFs) such as NF-L, NF-M, and NF-H (Malka-Gibor et al., 2017), which serve as signature markers for axons.
evidence: The claim is supported by established knowledge from published literature.

claim: Large expanses of endoplasmic reticulum (ER) cisternae extended into thin membrane tubules tightly associated with microtubules.
source: Furthermore, we frequently observed large expanses of endoplasmic reticulum (ER) cisternae, which extended into thin membrane tubules tightly associated with microtubules (Figure 2A, cyan arrows).
evidence: The claim is supported by cryo-ET observations shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Membrane contact sites between ER-mitochondria and ER-plasma membrane were observed.
source: We also observed membrane contact sites between ER-mitochondria and ER-plasma membrane (Figure 2B, white arrows).
evidence: The claim is supported by cryo-ET observations shown in Figure 2B.

claim: No obvious ultrastructural differences were observed between fGFP+ and GFP negative axons.
source: We did not observe any obvious ultrastructural differences between fGFP+ and GFP negative axons (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparative analysis of cryo-ET data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Approximately 17% of vesicles were associated with microtubules.
source: While most vesicles appeared free in the cytosol, approximately 17 % were associated with microtubules and 14 % with actin (N = 290, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of vesicle localization from cryo-ET data.

claim: Approximately 14% of vesicles were associated with actin.
source: While most vesicles appeared free in the cytosol, approximately 17 % were associated with microtubules and 14 % with actin (N = 290, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of vesicle localization from cryo-ET data.

claim: Free vesicles had mean diameters of about 52.00 nm (SD = 19.42 nm, N = 200).
source: The vesicles had mean diameters of about 50 nm (52.00 nm, SD = 19.42 nm, N = 200 for free vesicles; 50.92 nm, SD = 16.70 nm, N = 49 for MT associated vesicles, and 52.18 nm, SD = 17.84 nm, N = 41 for actin associated vesicles) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by measurements from cryo-ET data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Microtubule-associated vesicles had mean diameters of 50.92 nm (SD = 16.70 nm, N = 49).
source: The vesicles had mean diameters of about 50 nm (52.00 nm, SD = 19.42 nm, N = 200 for free vesicles; 50.92 nm, SD = 16.70 nm, N = 49 for MT associated vesicles, and 52.18 nm, SD = 17.84 nm, N = 41 for actin associated vesicles) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by measurements from cryo-ET data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Actin-associated vesicles had mean diameters of 52.18 nm (SD = 17.84 nm, N = 41).
source: The vesicles had mean diameters of about 50 nm (52.00 nm, SD = 19.42 nm, N = 200 for free vesicles; 50.92 nm, SD = 16.70 nm, N = 49 for MT associated vesicles, and 52.18 nm, SD = 17.84 nm, N = 41 for actin associated vesicles) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by measurements from cryo-ET data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Vesicle sizes in human axons are similar to vesicles in axons of mouse dorsal root ganglia neurons.
source: These sizes are similar to vesicles in axons of mouse dorsal root ganglia neurons (Foster et al., 2021b).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison to published data on mouse neurons.

claim: The majority of microtubule bundles had a uniform, parallel microtubule arrangement.
source: This analysis showed that the majority of bundles had a uniform, parallel microtubule arrangement, further confirming axon identity (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by subtomogram averaging analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The majority of microtubules consisted of 13 protofilaments.
source: We found that the majority of microtubules consisted of 13 protofilaments, while 2 microtubules had 12 protofilaments (N = 28) (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by subtomogram averaging analysis shown in Figure 3D and E.

claim: Two microtubules had 12 protofilaments (N = 28).
source: We found that the majority of microtubules consisted of 13 protofilaments, while 2 microtubules had 12 protofilaments (N = 28) (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by subtomogram averaging analysis shown in Figure 3D and E.

claim: 13 protofilaments have been suggested to be the predominant molecular architecture of microtubules in human cells.
source: Although we cannot exclude that the microtubule organization we observed was influenced or stabilized by labeling with SiR-tubulin in the subset of experiments where this labeling was performed, 13 protofilaments have been suggested before to be the predominant molecular architecture of microtubules in human cells (Watanabe et al., 2020; Chaaban and Brouhard, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by published literature on microtubule structure in human cells.

claim: The subtomogram average revealed the typical 4 nm repeat of individual tubulin subunits along the protofilaments.
source: We calculated a 3D subtomogram average from 16 of the 13-protofilament microtubules, which revealed the typical 4 nm repeat of individual tubulin subunits along the protofilaments (Figure 3—figure supplement 1; Amos and Klug, 1974; Nogales et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by subtomogram averaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and comparison to published structural data.

claim: Each micrometer of axon length on average corresponded to approximately 1.24 × 10^6 nm^2 of plasma membrane area (SD = 7.3 x 10^5 nm^2, N = 14).
source: Each micrometer of length on average corresponded to approximately 1.24 × 106 nm2 of plasma membrane area (SD = 7.3 x 105 nm2, N = 14) (Figure 3G).
evidence: The claim is supported by segmentation and surface area measurements from cryo-ET data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Each µm^2 of membrane contains approximately 5 × 10^6 lipids, corresponding to five lipid molecules/nm^2.
source: Because each µm2 of membrane contains approximately 5 × 106 lipids (Alberts et al., 2002), corresponding to five lipid molecules/nm2, we estimated the lipid supply to the plasma membrane required to sustain the average growth rate of an axon as approximately 4.3 × 106 lipid molecules/min.
evidence: The claim is supported by established knowledge from published literature.

claim: The lipid supply to the plasma membrane required to sustain the average growth rate of an axon is approximately 4.3 × 10^6 lipid molecules/min.
source: Because each µm2 of membrane contains approximately 5 × 106 lipids (Alberts et al., 2002), corresponding to five lipid molecules/nm2, we estimated the lipid supply to the plasma membrane required to sustain the average growth rate of an axon as approximately 4.3 × 106 lipid molecules/min.
evidence: The claim is supported by calculation based on measured growth rates and membrane area, combined with established knowledge from literature.

claim: ER tubules in axon shafts measured on average 10.8 nm (SD 2.0 nm, 82 measurements) at their thinnest outer diameter.
source: At their thinnest outer diameter, the ER tubules in axon shafts measured on average 10.8 nm (SD 2.0 nm, 82 measurements), which is narrower than previously observed in mouse axons (Terasaki, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by measurements from cryo-ET data and comparison to published data on mouse axons.

claim: ER tubules in axon shafts are narrower than previously observed in mouse axons.
source: At their thinnest outer diameter, the ER tubules in axon shafts measured on average 10.8 nm (SD 2.0 nm, 82 measurements), which is narrower than previously observed in mouse axons (Terasaki, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of measurements from cryo-ET data to published data on mouse axons.

claim: The thinnest ER tubules in HeLa cells measured about 20.4 nm (SD 3.2 nm, 24 measurements).
source: For comparison we measured the thinnest ER tubules in HeLa cells and found them to be about twice the diameter (20.4 nm, SD 3.2 nm, 24 measurements) (Figure 3H,I).
evidence: The claim is supported by measurements from cryo-ET data of HeLa cells shown in Figure 3H,I.

claim: Some axonal ER tubules had a local outer diameter of less than 10 nm.
source: Some of the axonal ER tubules had a local outer diameter of less than 10 nm.
evidence: The claim is supported by measurements from cryo-ET data.

claim: Axonal ER tubules contain hardly any lumenal space.
source: Considering that this measurement includes the bilayer thickness, this implies that these ER tubules of human axons contain hardly any lumenal space, likely posing constraints on diffusion of ER proteins.
evidence: The claim is inferred from measurements of ER tubule diameter and knowledge of bilayer thickness.

claim: The axonal ER structure may be a consequence of maximized synthesis of lipids, produced to sustain high growth rates during axon lengthening.
source: The observation that the ER is depleted of lumen whilst adopting highly curved tubular shapes indicates high local membrane surface-to-ER volume ratios, and suggests that the axonal ER structure may be a consequence of maximized synthesis of lipids, produced to sustain high growth rates during axon lengthening.
evidence: The claim is inferred from observations of ER structure and the high lipid demand for axon growth.

claim: A scarcity of potential ribosomes was observed within tomograms of growing axon shafts.
source: It was therefore noteworthy that we observed a scarcity of potential ribosomes within our tomograms of growing axon shafts.
evidence: The claim is supported by visual inspection and quantification of cryo-ET data.

claim: On average two ribosome-like particles per µm^3 were found in axon shafts (SD = 3 particles, n = 31 tomograms).
source: In order to assess the occurrence of ribosomes quantitatively, we counted ribosome-like particles, both cytosolic and membrane-bound, and found on average two particles per µm3 in axon shafts (SD = 3 particles, n = 31 tomograms), 589 particles per µm3 in other neuronal processes (SD = 344 particles, n = 4 tomograms), and 2314 particles per µm3 in HeLa cells (SD = 977 particles, n = 5 tomograms) (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of cryo-ET data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: 589 ribosome-like particles per µm^3 were found in other neuronal processes (SD = 344 particles, n = 4 tomograms).
source: In order to assess the occurrence of ribosomes quantitatively, we counted ribosome-like particles, both cytosolic and membrane-bound, and found on average two particles per µm3 in axon shafts (SD = 3 particles, n = 31 tomograms), 589 particles per µm3 in other neuronal processes (SD = 344 particles, n = 4 tomograms), and 2314 particles per µm3 in HeLa cells (SD = 977 particles, n = 5 tomograms) (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of cryo-ET data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: 2314 ribosome-like particles per µm^3 were found in HeLa cells (SD = 977 particles, n = 5 tomograms).
source: In order to assess the occurrence of ribosomes quantitatively, we counted ribosome-like particles, both cytosolic and membrane-bound, and found on average two particles per µm3 in axon shafts (SD = 3 particles, n = 31 tomograms), 589 particles per µm3 in other neuronal processes (SD = 344 particles, n = 4 tomograms), and 2314 particles per µm3 in HeLa cells (SD = 977 particles, n = 5 tomograms) (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of cryo-ET data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The local ribosome concentration in axon shafts is less than 3.5 nM, about 1000-fold lower than in HeLa cells.
source: The local ribosome concentration in axon shafts is thus less than 3.5 nM, about 1000-fold lower than in HeLa cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by calculation based on quantitative analysis of ribosome-like particles in cryo-ET data.

claim: The ribosome-like particles found in tomograms of axon shafts had an average diameter of 26.8 nm (SD = 3.7, N = 27).
source: The ribosome-like particles found in tomograms of axon shafts had an average diameter of 26.8 nm (SD = 3.7, N = 27), in agreement with the dimensions of human ribosomes (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B; Anger et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by measurements from cryo-ET data and comparison to published dimensions of human ribosomes.

claim: 11 ribosome-like particles were in close proximity to ER membrane.
source: 11 of them were in close proximity to ER membrane (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of cryo-ET data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Axon shafts identified as SMI312+/MAP2- showed significantly lower ribosomal signal than dendrites (SMI312-/MAP2+).
source: In agreement with the cryo-ET data, axon shafts identified as SMI312+/MAP2- showed significantly lower ribosomal signal than dendrites (SMI312-/MAP2+) (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The large amounts of axonal ER had a minute number of ribosomes attached.
source: Thus, the large amounts of axonal ER had a minute number of ribosomes attached, supporting the idea that the ER has a primary function in lipid metabolism rather than protein synthesis.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of ribosome-like particles in cryo-ET data.

claim: The ER has a primary function in lipid metabolism rather than protein synthesis in growing axon shafts.
source: Thus, the large amounts of axonal ER had a minute number of ribosomes attached, supporting the idea that the ER has a primary function in lipid metabolism rather than protein synthesis.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation of extensive ER with few attached ribosomes.

claim: Cryo-ET studies of neurons have been conducted on rodent primary cells grown on EM grids.
source: To date, cryo-ET studies of neurons have been conducted on rodent primary cells grown on EM grids (Tao et al., 2018; Garvalov et al., 2006; Lučić et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Dissociated neurons exhibit a random pattern of neurites, where axons typically grow along dendrites.
source: Such dissociated neurons exhibit a random pattern of neurites, where axons typically grow along dendrites and do not form the directed long-range tracts seen in the context of tissue.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about dissociated neuronal cultures.

claim: Cryo-EM of human neurons has so far remained out of reach.
source: Moreover, cryo-EM of human neurons has so far remained out of reach.
evidence: The claim is based on the state of the field prior to this study.

claim: The combination of human cerebral organoids with cryo-CLEM overcomes limitations of previous approaches.
source: We demonstrate that these limitations can be overcome by the combination of human cerebral organoids with cryo-CLEM.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental approach and results presented in the study.

claim: The organization of the cytoskeleton, in particular the dense microtubule bundles, likely reflects the importance of mechanical properties and cytoskeletal transport for projection of axons over long distances.
source: The organization of the cytoskeleton, in particular the dense microtubule bundles, likely reflects the importance of mechanical properties, such as rigidity, and of cytoskeletal transport for projection of axons over long distances.
evidence: The claim is inferred from observations of cytoskeletal organization in cryo-ET data.

claim: Growing axon shafts contain exclusively smooth ER, similarly to mature nervous tissue.
source: Growing axon shafts also appear to contain exclusively smooth ER, similarly to mature nervous tissue depicted in textbook electron micrographs.
evidence: The claim is supported by observations from cryo-ET data and comparison to established knowledge.

claim: The tight association of the ER with microtubules could reflect attachment needed to pull the ER along the extending axon.
source: Furthermore, the tight association of the ER with microtubules could reflect attachment needed to pull the ER along the extending axon.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on observations of ER-microtubule association.

claim: The tight association of the ER with microtubules could represent piercing of ER cisternae by microtubules that grow quickly along the extending axon.
source: Alternatively, this arrangement could represent piercing of ER cisternae by microtubules that grow quickly along the extending axon.
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing an alternative explanation for ER-microtubule association.

claim: Previous EM studies have reported clusters of ribosomes in the axon initial segment and growth cones.
source: Previous EM studies have reported clusters of ribosomes in the axon initial segment and growth cones (Bartlett and Banker, 1984; Tennyson, 1970; Yamada et al., 1971; Bunge, 1973; Steward and Ribak, 1986; Koenig et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Mature presynaptic termini harbor ribosomal components, consistent with the presence of a distal ribosome pool.
source: Mature presynaptic termini were shown to harbor ribosomal components, consistent with the presence of a distal ribosome pool, and metabolic labeling experiments demonstrated presynaptic protein synthesis (Hafner et al., 2019; Shigeoka et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Metabolic labeling experiments demonstrated presynaptic protein synthesis.
source: Mature presynaptic termini were shown to harbor ribosomal components, consistent with the presence of a distal ribosome pool, and metabolic labeling experiments demonstrated presynaptic protein synthesis (Hafner et al., 2019; Shigeoka et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The shafts of developing axons specifically exhibit low ribosome numbers.
source: Our findings reveal that the shafts of developing axons specifically exhibit low ribosome numbers.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of ribosome-like particles in cryo-ET data.

claim: Different regions of the axon can exhibit very different supramolecular landscapes.
source: These observations complement previous findings of local translation at growth cones and presynaptic termini, and suggest that different regions of the axon can exhibit very different supramolecular landscapes.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the current findings and previous literature on local translation.

claim: Biological processes in the axon initial segment, the growth cone, and presynaptic termini rely on local translation.
source: We therefore propose a refined model in which biological processes in the axon initial segment, the growth cone, and presynaptic termini rely on local translation (Bartlett and Banker, 1984; Yamada et al., 1971; Tennyson, 1970; Bunge, 1973; Steward and Ribak, 1986; Koenig et al., 2000; Hafner et al., 2019; Shigeoka et al., 2016), while the axon shaft during growth is depleted of translational machinery and thus displays limited capacity for new protein synthesis.
evidence: The claim is a proposed model based on current findings and previous literature.

claim: The axon shaft during growth is depleted of translational machinery and thus displays limited capacity for new protein synthesis.
source: We therefore propose a refined model in which biological processes in the axon initial segment, the growth cone, and presynaptic termini rely on local translation (Bartlett and Banker, 1984; Yamada et al., 1971; Tennyson, 1970; Bunge, 1973; Steward and Ribak, 1986; Koenig et al., 2000; Hafner et al., 2019; Shigeoka et al., 2016), while the axon shaft during growth is depleted of translational machinery and thus displays limited capacity for new protein synthesis.
evidence: The claim is a proposed model based on current findings.

claim: Protein synthesis in the growth cone was previously shown to be used primarily for navigation and not for extension.
source: Furthermore, because protein synthesis in the growth cone was previously shown to be used primarily for navigation and not for extension (Campbell and Holt, 2001), ribosomal depletion along the shaft might represent a mechanism to desensitize this structure to exogenous guidance cues and ensure correct wiring.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Ribosomal depletion along the shaft might represent a mechanism to desensitize this structure to exogenous guidance cues and ensure correct wiring.
source: Furthermore, because protein synthesis in the growth cone was previously shown to be used primarily for navigation and not for extension (Campbell and Holt, 2001), ribosomal depletion along the shaft might represent a mechanism to desensitize this structure to exogenous guidance cues and ensure correct wiring.
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing a functional interpretation of ribosome depletion.

claim: The combination of cryo-CLEM and human cerebral organoid technology is a powerful method to address the cell biology and architecture of neuronal compartments.
source: Overall, these findings demonstrate that the combination of cryo-CLEM and human cerebral organoid technology is a powerful method to address the cell biology and architecture of its compartments.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental approach and results presented in the study.

claim: This approach is not limited to axons and could be extended to other organoid-derived cell types as long as the preparation allows sample vitrification.
source: Conceptually this approach is not limited to axons and could be extended to other organoid-derived cell types as long as the preparation allows sample vitrification.
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing potential extensions of the methodology.

claim: This methodology could potentially be applied to blood vessel organoids to study ultrastructural aspects of vasculature development and vasculopathy.
source: For instance, this methodology could potentially be applied to blood vessel organoids (Wimmer et al., 2019) to study ultrastructural aspects of vasculature development and vasculopathy, since, like neurons, the developing vasculature extends long, thin structures that would be amenable to vitrification in the same manner.
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing a potential application of the methodology.

claim: One could place neural crest organoids in close proximity to EM grids to capture neural crest cells and study their ultrastructure during migration and differentiation.
source: For example, one could place neural crest organoids (Foltz et al., 2021) in close proximity to EM grids to capture neural crest cells and study their ultrastructure during migration and differentiation into different neural crest cell derivatives.
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing a potential application of the methodology.

claim: The combination of cerebral organoid technology and cryo-ET provides a window into the architecture of the human axonal compartment.
source: In conclusion, the combination of cerebral organoid technology and cryo-ET provides a window into the architecture of the human axonal compartment.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental approach and results presented in the study.

claim: This methodology holds the potential to further our understanding of neuronal development, neurodegeneration and nerve injury.
source: We believe this methodology holds the potential to further our understanding of neuronal development, neurodegeneration and nerve injury.
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing potential future applications of the methodology.

claim: High-pressure freezing followed by freeze-substitution results in improved preservation of mouse nervous tissue compared to chemical fixation.
source: In comparison to chemical fixation, high-pressure freezing followed by freeze-substitution was shown to result in improved preservation of mouse nervous tissue, highlighting the importance of cryo-fixation for a more accurate interpretation of ultrastructural details (Korogod et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: The combination of cryo-fixation with EM imaging at cryogenic temperatures is particularly suited to preserve the fine structure of neuronal cells.
source: The combination of cryo-fixation with EM imaging at cryogenic temperatures is particularly suited to preserve the fine structure of neuronal cells (Lučić et al., 2007; Fernández-Busnadiego et al., 2010; Zuber et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Recent methodological advances in cryo-ET and subtomogram averaging have enabled in situ structural studies of protein complexes within their cellular context.
source: Furthermore, recent methodological advances in cryo-ET and subtomogram averaging have enabled in situ structural studies of protein complexes within their cellular context (O'Reilly et al., 2020; Tegunov et al., 2021; Watanabe et al., 2020; Allegretti et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Cerebral organoids provide the opportunity to study aspects of human neuronal physiology within the context of a complex 3D cellular milieu mimicking the architecture of the developing brain.
source: Cerebral organoids provide the opportunity to study aspects of human neuronal physiology within the context of a complex 3D cellular milieu mimicking the architecture of the developing brain (Birey et al., 2017; Lancaster et al., 2017; Quadrato et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: An optimized air-liquid interface slice culture paradigm enables long-term culture of cerebral organoids and promotes the establishment of axon tracts.
source: Recently, we developed an optimized air-liquid interface slice culture paradigm (Giandomenico et al., 2019) that enables long-term culture of cerebral organoids and promotes the establishment of axon tracts, consisting of dozens or, in thicker tracts, even up to thousands of individual axons bundled together, able to form functional connections.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Corticofugal axon tracts project over long distances of several millimeters from the organoid.
source: While the cell bodies are part of the organoid tissue, corticofugal (deep-layer identity) axon tracts project over long distances of several millimeters from the organoid (Giandomenico et al., 2019), effectively segregating the axons from dendrites and somata.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: The separation between plasma membranes of adjacent axons within tracts was remarkably narrow.
source: While the separation between plasma membranes of adjacent axons within tracts was remarkably narrow, we found no significant difference between cell-cell contacts from fGFP and L1CAM-GFP overexpressing ALI-COs (fGFP: mean = 5.63 nm, SD = 0.65 nm, N = 25 and L1CAM-GFP: mean = 5.29 nm, SD = 0.58 nm, N = 9) (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by measurements from cryo-ET data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

claim: No significant difference was found between cell-cell contacts from fGFP and L1CAM-GFP overexpressing ALI-COs (fGFP: mean = 5.63 nm, SD = 0.65 nm, N = 25 and L1CAM-GFP: mean = 5.29 nm, SD = 0.58 nm, N = 9).
source: While the separation between plasma membranes of adjacent axons within tracts was remarkably narrow, we found no significant difference between cell-cell contacts from fGFP and L1CAM-GFP overexpressing ALI-COs (fGFP: mean = 5.63 nm, SD = 0.65 nm, N = 25 and L1CAM-GFP: mean = 5.29 nm, SD = 0.58 nm, N = 9) (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of measurements from cryo-ET data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

claim: 86% of fGFP tomograms (N = 22) contained at least one instance in which the ER was within approximately 30 nm distance from the plasma membrane.
source: The frequency with which we observed such contact sites was similar in both data sets (86 % of fGFP tomograms (N = 22) and 90 % of GFP-ESYT1 tomograms (N = 10) contained at least one instance in which the ER was within approximately 30 nm distance from the plasma membrane) (examples in Figure 2—figure supplement 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of ER-plasma membrane contact sites in cryo-ET data.

claim: 90% of GFP-ESYT1 tomograms (N = 10) contained at least one instance in which the ER was within approximately 30 nm distance from the plasma membrane.
source: The frequency with which we observed such contact sites was similar in both data sets (86 % of fGFP tomograms (N = 22) and 90 % of GFP-ESYT1 tomograms (N = 10) contained at least one instance in which the ER was within approximately 30 nm distance from the plasma membrane) (examples in Figure 2—figure supplement 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of ER-plasma membrane contact sites in cryo-ET data.

claim: Membrane contact sites between the ER and the plasma membrane likely represent sites for transfer of newly synthesized lipid molecules.
source: In addition, we observed membrane contact sites between the ER and the plasma membrane, likely representing sites for transfer of newly synthesized lipid molecules, as lipid flux is a major function of membrane contact sites (Levine, 2004; Prinz, 2014).
evidence: The claim is inferred from observations and supported by citations to published literature on membrane contact site function.

claim: Lipid flux is a major function of membrane contact sites.
source: In addition, we observed membrane contact sites between the ER and the plasma membrane, likely representing sites for transfer of newly synthesized lipid molecules, as lipid flux is a major function of membrane contact sites (Levine, 2004; Prinz, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The time from detachment until completed cryo-fixation was kept as short as possible and within less than 20 s.
source: Detachment and plunge-freezing were coordinated between two experimenters who sequentially handled the grids, to keep the time from detachment until completed cryo-fixation as short as possible and within less than 20 s (see Materials and methods).
evidence: The claim is supported by description of the experimental procedure.
